segments.source: A local choice can block a later assignment, so the whole matching must be checked.
Good reasoning includes checking how informative, robust, falsifiable, causal, or dominated a conclusion is.

Four equally likely locations A,B,C,D remain possible. Question Q1 asks “Is it A?”; Q2 asks “Is it A or B?” A yes/no question is more balanced when its two answer branches contain more nearly equal numbers of possibilities. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 3 km and two checkpoints are 8 cm apart.
Use branch sizes as the information criterion in this exercise. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.
Which question is more balanced and therefore more informative by the stated criterion? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?
1. Q1 splits the four possibilities 1 versus 3. 2. Q2 splits them 2 versus 2. 3. The 2–2 split is more balanced. Cross-domain check: 8×3=24 km.
A result can be numerically correct yet epistemically weak; meta-reasoning evaluates the quality of the inference itself.
Meta-level predicate over hypotheses or decisions: information balance, robustness, counterexample, causality, or dominance.
Good reasoning includes checking how informative, robust, falsifiable, causal, or dominated a conclusion is.

Option A scores between 49 and 53 after measurement error; option B scores between 50 and 52. A ranking is robust only if every allowed value of A remains above every allowed value of B. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 8:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.
Test worst cases: robust A>B requires min(A)>max(B). For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.
Is the ranking A>B robust? Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?
1. min(A)=49; max(B)=52. 2. 49>52 is false. 3. Some allowed values reverse the ranking. Cross-domain check: 8+2=10, so the team finishes at 10:00.
No; the ranking is sensitive to the uncertainty. Cross-domain answer: 10:00.

Claim: “Every town with more roads has shorter average travel time.” Town X has 6 roads and average travel time 35 minutes. Town Y has 4 roads and average travel time 20 minutes. Cross-domain check: a local committee has 11 members, requires at least 6 present for quorum, and 11 are present.
A universal claim is disproved by one case that satisfies its condition but not its conclusion. For the cross-domain check, quorum exists when present members ≥ the stated threshold.
Do X and Y provide a counterexample to the claim? Cross-domain check: is quorum met?
1. X has more roads than Y. 2. Yet X has longer, not shorter, travel time. 3. Therefore the universal claim fails on this pair. Cross-domain check: compare 11 with 6; 11≥6 is true.
Yes. X and Y form a counterexample. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.

Across several months, ice-cream sales and sunburn cases rise together. Temperature also rises in those months. No intervention is described. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 15 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.
Correlation between X and Y does not by itself prove X causes Y; a third variable may influence both. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.
